the rule is HASHED before it arrives (`scopeKeyPrefix`'s idiom), never abbreviated. A test asserts that no
value is path-shaped, so the day someone publishes `logsDir` is the day that test goes red.

**`tz` is here because a cron pattern has no timezone.** `triggers.json` carries no `tz` field on a cron
entry and BullMQ hands the pattern to cron-parser with no zone, so it resolves in each worker's LOCAL
system time. On one host that is exactly what an operator means. On two hosts in different zones the same
pattern is two different instants, with nothing anywhere saying so -- unlike `pause-windows.json`, whose
every window carries an explicit `tz` and is therefore already fleet-correct.

**`fpUsd` is numbers and counter hashes only** (issue #501, part 6). The dollar counters (`budget:usd:*`) are
shared keys, but each host reads its caps from its own env, overlay and scoped-limits file, so two hosts can judge
one counter against two caps. `fpUsd` is `fingerprint.mjs`'s 16-hex digest of: the four dollar settings
(`maxCostUsd`, `dailyCostUsd`, `weeklyCostUsd`, `monthlyCostUsd`) as integer micro-dollars or null, the overlay
over env as a job resolves them (with an invalid overlay, or merged values that break the dollar rule, the env
values; such a host refuses every job as `settings-overlay-invalid`); every scoped-limits row that carries a dollar
window, as its counter prefix (`budget:usd:s:<hash16>` or `budget:usd:mdl:<hash16>`) and its three caps in
micro-dollars, sorted by prefix; and the sorted counter prefixes of the model rows a job with no list of its own
reserves in under `PI_ALLOWED_MODELS` (every model row when it is unset). Never a scope string, a model id, a value
as written or an amount in clear: the input holds only integers, nulls, the word `invalid` for an amount that does
not parse, and the prefixes. Published
as a thunk, so an overlay or scoped-limits edit shows within one beat; an env change needs the restart it always
needs. It never ABSTAINS, unlike `fpCron`: a host with no dollar setting publishes the empty fingerprint, because a
host that reserves no dollars against a counter its peers cap is the disagreement worth seeing. Only `doctor` reads
it, and only to WARN (`dollar-fingerprint.mjs`, `doctor.mjs -> fleetDollarChecks`): a host that differs, or one that
publishes none while dollar caps are in use, which is this host's or a peer's published fingerprint not being the
empty one, or else a dollar counter found on the Valkey (best effort, asked only then: `EXISTS` on the deployment's
current day, week and month keys, then a bounded `SCAN` for `budget:usd:*`, within two seconds; a capped host from
before `fpUsd` leaves its counters, but a host with only a per-job cap leaves no counter). Nothing refuses on it.

**`fpProjects` is ids and member hashes only** (issue #499 part C). Each host resolves a job's project from its own
`projects.json` while the project rows' counters are shared, so two copies put one repo in two projects, or in a
project on one host and in none on another. `fpProjects` is `fingerprint.mjs`'s 16-hex digest of the projects sorted
by id, each as its id and the sorted 16-hex hash (`hash16`) of each member: never a `name` (free text that decides
nothing) and never a member in clear (a folder member is a host path, a repo member a repository name). A separate
field rather than a part of `fpUsd`, deliberately: membership decides the job-count project rows and the recorded
project as well as the dollar rows, so it matters on a fleet that sets no dollar cap, and one warning that says
"projects" names the file to copy where a dollar warning would send the operator to the wrong one. Published as a
thunk over the live projects ref, so an edit shows within one beat. It never ABSTAINS: a host with no projects file
publishes the digest of no projects. Only `doctor` reads it, to WARN (`doctor.mjs -> fleetProjectsChecks`): a peer
whose digest differs, or one that publishes none while projects are in use (this host's or a peer's digest is not the
one of no projects). When this host's own projects file does not load, doctor fails on that and makes no comparison,
so a healthy peer is not blamed. Nothing refuses on it.

**`fpEnvelope` is a digest or the word `none`** (issue #504 part B). It is `envelopeDigest` of the host's LIVE
envelope (`INT-ENVELOPE-FILE-CONTRACT`'s normalized form, 16 hex), published as a thunk so a reload shows within one
beat, or `none` when `PI_ENVELOPE_FILE` is unset. A name rather than an empty value, so a host without an envelope is
told apart from a worker too old to publish the field. It is NOT what the refusal reads: a host refuses governed jobs
as `envelope-mismatch` by comparing its own digest with the applied split's (`alloc:plan`), never a peer's row, so
deleting the keyspace changes no decision. Only `doctor` reads it. Doctor reads the applied split (`alloc:plan`, one
GET) whenever it may talk to the Valkey; with one present it prints the split's envelope digest, names the hosts whose
`fpEnvelope` matches it (a warning, not a green line, when none does), and FAILS for this host and for each peer whose
value differs, `none` included, since each refuses its governed jobs; every such line names its host, this host's as
`this host (<PI_WORKER_NAME>)` (issue #507), so a fleet's doctor outputs read side by side say which host refuses; a key that does not decode is said as such and
counts as governed for a host with no envelope (`doctor.mjs -> appliedSplitChecks`). With no key, nothing is said. With
none, it WARNS about the peers whose digest differs from this host's
(`fleetEnvelopeChecks`) and about a peer that publishes no `fpEnvelope` field (a worker from before it) while an
envelope is in use somewhere (this host's or a peer's value is not `none`). When this host's own envelope does not
load, doctor fails on that and makes no comparison.

**`limitsVersion` is an integer** (issue #596). It is the build's `SCOPED_LIMITS_VERSION`, so a row without it is a
worker from before job sizes. A build refuses a newer scoped-limits file only when it loads one at boot; while it runs
it keeps its last good file on reload, so once the file is version 3 such a worker applies NEITHER the size NOR any
later edit to the file (job counts, `concurrent`, dollar caps) until it is upgraded and restarted, and says nothing on
the job. Only `doctor` reads the field, to WARN (`doctor.mjs -> fleetSizeChecks`): when this host's own file is
version 3 (it DECLARES 3, as an older build judges it, or a row carries a size), each peer whose `limitsVersion` is
absent or below 3 is named, with "upgrade and restart every worker" as the fix. When this host's file does not load, nothing is compared. Nothing
refuses on it.

**The host budget fields are integers, `off` or empty** (issue #596, phase 2, `DES-HOST-BUDGET`). Each is a thunk over
the worker's one budget, so every beat says what is held now. Two readers. `doctor` shows per host its budget, what
its jobs hold and the largest project size that fits it, per project the hosts it fits on, a warning per host whose
budget is below the projects' minimums together, and holds THIS host's `usedMemMiB` and `usedCpuCenti` against the
`pi.dispatch.mem` and `pi.dispatch.cpu` labels of the job containers its runtime lists (a warning when they differ or
a container carries none), and warns when THIS host's `budgetSeed` is `unlisted`, naming the venues. NO JOB DECISION READS THEM. An
earlier draft of phase 2 refused a forge job `job-size-exceeds-fleet` after two reads 30 s apart showed no live host
whose budget fits it, and the gate round refuted it: a clean stop DELETES its row, a crash lets it expire, and
`readLiveHosts` drops a row whose read times out, so a host that is merely restarting was read as absent and a job it
would have run was refused for good. A job on the shared queue of a host with `PI_WORKER_NAME` whose size never fits this host
now waits for a host it fits on (a host without one refuses it: nobody else drains its queue), and doctor names a project that fits no live host. So the falsification test below holds UNAMENDED again.

**The TTL is refreshed on EVERY beat**, which reverses this project's stated set-once rule (`budget.mjs`:
*"set the TTL only when the key is first created, so a long window cannot push its expiry forward"*). The
reversal is correct because the OBJECT differs: a COUNTER whose TTL refreshes on every increment stops
being a window, while a LEASE's expiry IS its liveness claim, so refreshing it is the mechanism rather
than a leak. The in-repo precedent is lease-shaped -- `wait-state.hold` re-`PEXPIRE`s the supersede lease,
and only after checking the lease is still its own, which this key gets for free by being named after its
only writer.

**A clean shutdown DELETES the row** rather than letting it expire, so the TTL only ever covers a crash
and a rolling restart leaves no ghost peer behind. `wait-state.release` takes the same posture.

**Once `close()` has been ENTERED, this module writes no log line and adds nothing back to the index**,
and the flag rather than the drain is what delivers it (issue #302). `close` drains with one
`bounded(inFlight, timeoutMs)` while `write` spends one bound per command, so a write can outlive the
drain: measured against a stalled Valkey, `host_registry_unreachable` landed 76ms and
`host_registry_restored` 108ms after `close()` had RESOLVED, through the closure of a boot that had
stopped, and a late `SADD` put the name back into `host:live` 40ms after the same `close`'s `SREM` took it
out. The drain deliberately stays at one `timeoutMs`, because widening it to `write`'s worst case would
triple a shutdown bound whose whole point is to be short; both of `beat`'s transition arms and the `SADD`
are gated on `closed` instead. This is `DES-WATCHERS-CLOSE-WITH-THE-WORKER`'s rule reached from the other
side: work already in flight cannot be recalled, so what a close gates is its VOICE.

Of the module's three log sites, two are gated and the third **cannot be late**, which is what makes the
absolute wording above true rather than approximate: `host_registry_field_refused` is emitted by `write`'s
field loop, which runs synchronously inside `beat`'s own entry check before the first `await`. The `PEXPIRE`
is deliberately NOT gated beside the `SADD`, and the asymmetry is the point. The `SADD` is an index write
that `close`'s `SREM` undoes, so repeating it after a close resurrects a ghost; the `PEXPIRE` is the row's
own fuse, and skipping it on a close that landed between the `HSET` and the `PEXPIRE` leaves
`host:h:<name>` with NO expiry at all. That row is invisible, because every reader walks `host:live` and
the `SREM` emptied it, so it is a keyspace leak rather than a ghost peer and the reader's prune never
reaches it. The fuse is only as good as the write that lights it, and that bound predates this change: a
FIRST beat whose `HSET` landed while its reply was lost past the bound dies before the `PEXPIRE` is ever
issued, so a `DEL` lost at shutdown leaves the same TTL-less row with or without any gate -- measured on a
live server, `PTTL -1` on the pre-#302 code and the fixed code alike. A server-outage residual of the
bounded-write design, recorded beside the fix so the asymmetry above is not read as a guarantee.

**The index leak is handled by the READER**, exactly as `wait:held`'s is and for the measured reason
recorded there: a SET cannot expire its members, and the alternative -- no index and a `SCAN host:h:*`
instead -- walks HARDEST on deployments with nothing to show, because the early exit never fires, while
the panel reads every second.

**A member outside the worker name charset is no host's** (issue #737, PR 3b, ADDED 2026-10-25). `readLiveHosts` skips
a `host:live` member that fails `WORKER_NAME_RE` (the worker name charset: a letter or a digit, then letters, digits,
`.`, `_` and `-`, at most 64 characters in all; looser than the boot rule, which also refuses a `.json` or `.log` tail
on `PI_WORKER_NAME`, `config.mjs`, so a member such as `prod.json` is still read) before it reads that member's row,
and skips a row whose own `name` fails the same charset (an empty `name` still stands for the member). It prunes
neither, a pruning reader included: anything with the Valkey's URL can SADD a member, removing what someone else wrote
is not a reader's call, and such a member costs only its place in the set. A reader that took one would print it
wherever rows are drawn: a 3,000-character member widened the console's page to 43,000 px. Every consumer reads
through `readLiveHosts` (the cron gate through `livePeers`), so none of them is handed such a row, and the
falsification test holds unamended (a skipped member was never a host).

**`{ unreachable }` and `[]` are different answers** and no consumer may collapse them. "There are no
other hosts" and "I could not find out" differ, and a panel that renders the second as the first tells an
operator their fleet is gone when Valkey merely blinked.

**The two shared bounds keep their keys under the prefixes they belong to**, not under `host:`:
`wait:check:<i>` sits with the rest of the wait feature so one `KEYS wait:*` still shows all of it, and
`slot:s:<16hex>:<i>` deliberately mirrors `budget:s:<16hex>` -- the same `scopeKeyPrefix` hash, so an
operator reading both keys for one scope sees the same sixteen characters. A row's money windows and its
concurrency are now both fleet-wide, by different mechanisms, and the difference is worth stating: a run
CAP counts events that already happened and must never be forgotten, while a concurrency SLOT describes
something happening now and must be forgotten when it stops. One is a ledger, the other a lease.

**A fact may be published as a VALUE or as a THUNK**, and the thunk is not a convenience. A fact that
can change without a restart -- the cron fingerprint after a live triggers-file edit, the live
concurrency after an overlay change -- must be re-read on every beat. Frozen at the call that started
the heartbeat, a peer would compare against what this host believed at BOOT, and after any edit the
two hosts' fingerprints would oscillate on the beat period: refusing or agreeing depending on which
half of a beat a reload happened to land in. A thunk that throws yields an absent field and never
skips the beat.

**`fpCron: ""` means ABSTAIN, not "no schedules"**, and the distinction is load-bearing rather than
pedantic. A worker with cron disabled has no view of what should be scheduled and must never be able
to disagree with one that does; a worker whose triggers file declares zero cron entries HAS a view,
and it is the sharpest form of the failure the gate exists to close.

**Every value is written through a bound, because the failure mode of this client is a HANG.**
`makeRedisClient` sets `maxRetriesPerRequest: null`, which BullMQ's blocking connections require and
which means a command issued against an unreachable server QUEUES rather than rejects. A `try/catch`
around it therefore catches nothing: an outage is not an exception. Every await here is bounded, which
is what converts "never answers" into "answered no" so the fail-open path can run at all -- and it is
why the unreachable transition is reportable rather than invisible. The bound's timer is deliberately
NOT unref'd: an unref'd timer does not fire when the hung command is the last thing holding the loop,
which is exactly the shutdown case the bound exists for.

**The content rule is enforced by the WRITER**, not by a test. A test can only check the fields it
publishes itself, so it could never catch the day a path is added at a real call site. A value with a
leading separator, a backslash, or a drive letter is DROPPED and named (`host_registry_field_refused`).
The rule is mechanical rather than a ban on `/`, because one admissible value contains one: an IANA
zone is `Europe/Amsterdam`. What no admissible value has is a filesystem ROOT.

**Residual, recorded rather than fixed**: a hostname whose characters are all outside the name charset
sanitizes to the same fallback on every such machine, so two hosts could share one row, one BullMQ
name and one record value -- the precise failure identity exists to prevent. An operator on such a
host declares `PI_WORKER_NAME`; nothing detects the collision yet.

**The falsification test for anything added here later**: DELETE THE WHOLE `host:*` KEYSPACE WHILE THE
FLEET RUNS, and every host must behave exactly as it did before this contract existed. That holds because
absence is read as "no peers", which is the single-host behaviour. Issue #596 phase 2 briefly let one decision read
the rows (a fleet refusal of a job too big for every listed host), and its gate round removed it, because absence
CAN cause that refusal (a restarting host is absent); the host budget fields are read by doctor only. `jobs`, `jobsMore`
and `waiters` (issue #599) are read by the capacity report only: deleting them loses the running jobs' share of a
report until the next beat, and no decision. A Redis-side toggle fails that test --
deleting it loses the operator's edit -- which is precisely why `OQ-008` refuses one, and why this
keyspace is not that.

**Doctor's published results are a separate keyspace** (AMENDED 2026-10-21, #712): `doctor:hosts` and
`doctor:h:<name>` (`INT-DOCTOR-RESULTS-KEY`), named by the same worker name as `host:h:<name>` but written by doctor,
not by the beat, and kept 7 days rather than 90 seconds, so a host that stopped beating still says what its last
doctor run found. They obey the same falsification test: deleting every `doctor:*` key while the fleet runs changes
no host's behaviour, because nothing reads them to decide anything. A registry row gains no field for them, and the
admin reads them for the live hosts' names beside the index's, so a lost index entry costs nothing.

## INT-CANCEL-CHANNEL-CONTRACT

- **Agent origin (#766)**: Delegated cancellations use `cancel:agent:req:<jobId>` with fixed value `agent-cancel` and `cancel:agent:ack:<jobId>`, with the same request/ack TTL and timeout cleanup. Human requests retain the original keys. The worker checks human then agent requests, acknowledges only the chosen channel and records the fixed matching reason. An older worker cannot misread an agent cancellation as a human intervention; it leaves the new request unanswered, a named timeout. A tool with an interactive human confirmation uses human origin independently of its audit role `agent`. Agent-only removals and cancellations produce no zero-touch stop event; draft helpers are never workload denominators.

**Producer of a request**: the CLI's `cancel` verb or the panel's `x` confirm. **Consumer**: the ONE
worker process holding the job -- BullMQ's `cancelJob` aborts an in-process map entry, returns `false`
silently for a job the process does not hold, and nothing anywhere maps a jobId to a host, so an active
job can only be stopped by asking whichever worker owns it to raise its own abort (issue #287).

```
  cancel:req:<jobId>   STRING "operator-cancel", TTL 60s -- the ask. Written by the requester; consumed
                       (DEL) by the owning worker after it raised the abort; DEL'd by the requester itself
                       on its own ack timeout, so a cancel the operator was told failed cannot fire a
                       minute later. The TTL reaps a requester that died mid-poll.
  cancel:ack:<jobId>   STRING <workerName> ("" on an undeclared host; a NAME, never a path, the
                       INT-HOST-REGISTRY-CONTRACT content rule), TTL 5m -- the answer the requester polls
                       for. No ack within the window is a NAMED refusal at the requester ("no worker
                       acknowledged ... nothing was changed"), never a silent no-op.
```

- **The worker side is a per-active-job poll beside the kill timer** (2s cadence, unref'd, cleared in the
  same finally that clears the timer), NOT a subscription: pub/sub is a connection type this repo has
  zero of, its fire-and-forget loses a cancel across a restart with no error anywhere, and the ack needs
  a readable key regardless. The poll is armed only when the injected redis has `get` -- a bare test
  wiring passes `{ incr, expire }` and arms nothing, byte-identically. Each tick swallows redis faults: a
  blip may cost the ack, never the job.
- **The reason string rides the abort**: `cancelJob(id, "operator-cancel")` becomes `signal.reason`,
  mapped onto the aborted runContainer result as `abortReason` at the one seam both abort paths flow
  through, and classified by the CLOSED exact-match `INT-RUNNER-EXIT-CODE-PROTOCOL` records. The record
  gains `reason: "operator-cancel"` and nothing else: `abortReason` itself never reaches `buildRecord`'s
  explicit literal (pinned).
- **State dispatch at the requester** (`cancel-cli.mjs`, seams throughout): held (a `wait:job:` hash with
  a `since` clock) goes through the shared `removeHeldJob` FIRST, because a held job IS delayed and the
  plain path would strand its hold keys as a lying panel row; plain delayed/waiting/prioritized gets
  `job.remove()` (a mid-dispatch pickup re-reads the state and falls through to the channel, since
  `remove()` throws on a locked job); active gets the request/ack poll above; completed/failed refuse.
  Queued and held cancels write NO run record -- the job never ran, the `dispatch_wait_cancel` rule --
  and the CLI says so in its output. AMENDED 2026-10-25 (#737, PR 3a): the held and the queued branches are
  ONE function, `removeQueuedJob({ redis, queue, job, jobId, state, guard })` in `cancel-state.mjs`, placed after
  `removeHeldJob` and calling it, which the console's `cancel-queued` runs too, so the two doors cannot drift. The
  CLI's output has one new line, for a held job whose removal failed after its hold was cleared (below): "could not
  cancel held job <id>: its hold was cleared, but the job itself could not be removed (<the error>); it may still be
  queued, now without its hold. Run `pi-dispatch cancel <id>` again to remove or stop it", an `error:` line on stderr
  with exit 1, where it said "could not cancel held job <id>: <the error>". And every line that carries another
  module's words carries them bounded (`boundedText` in `cancel-cli.mjs`), since they are of any length and any bytes
  on a terminal: each C0, DEL and C1 character made a space, then at most 200 characters of them. Those are the
  registry's words in "no job <id> in <n> queue(s) [registry unreadable: <its words> ...]", a removal's in the
  cleared line, in "could not cancel held job <id>: <the error>" and in "could not remove <id> ... the remove failed
  with: <the error>", and the error under the could-not-reach line (a lookup's, or anything else that threw). So, but
  for the new line, a line whose words hold none of those characters and are at most 200 characters long is byte for
  byte what it was, as is every line that carries none (a thrown value that is not an Error and has no message now reads
  "no reason given"); the worker's name in "cancel accepted by <host>", read from the ack key, is bounded the same way.
  It judges the hold first by the hash's `since` (a hash that cannot be read is no hold, as the CLI always read it),
  else removes a job in `QUEUED_STATES` (`delayed`, `waiting`, `prioritized`, `paused`), else changes nothing.
  `guard` is optional (the CLI passes none): a caller's last check, asked with the job right before the removal is
  sent (before `removeHeldJob` for a held job; after the state check and before `remove()` otherwise), which answers
  null to go on or what to refuse with, a throw refusing too; BullMQ's remove checks only the job's lock and its
  scheduler, so a caller whose rule is about what the job has DONE reads that again here. It answers
  `{ ok, held: true, jobId, attemptsMade }`, `{ invalid }` (removeHeldJob's refusal, nothing changed),
  `{ invalid, cleared: true }` (removeHeldJob failed once its hold's first key had been sent for deletion, most often
  `remove()` refusing a job a worker locked in between: the hold is gone, or partly gone, and the job stayed, which a
  caller never words as nothing changed; a first delete that failed, whatever the error, is followed by a read of the
  hold's clock (`HEXISTS wait:job:<id> since`, `holdInPlace`), and only a hold read back in place answers `{ invalid }`,
  nothing changed (Valkey refused the command, such as NOPERM, READONLY or MISCONF); a hold not read back, a read
  that fails, or a client with no `hexists` keeps the mark, since a refusal can be the answer to ioredis's resend,
  after a reconnect, of a delete that already ran), `{ refused, error? }` (the guard's answer, or its throw as
  `error` with `refused` null; nothing was sent), `{ notQueued, state }`, `{ ok, held: false, jobId, state,
  attemptsMade }` or `{ raced, state, error }` (`remove()` threw: a worker took the job between the read and the
  remove, or it is a job scheduler's next run, which BullMQ refuses to remove; the state read again), and never
  throws. Once a job is removed, and only then, it deletes the job's defer record (`DEL defer:job:<jobId>`,
  `INT-DEFER-REASON-KEY`): bounded (2 s), best effort (a failed delete leaves the record to its TTL, and a record
  whose job is gone is never read), and only where the client has `del`; a job that stays keeps its reason. WHO may
  be removed stays each caller's rule: the CLI also removes a job waiting to retry, and the console's `cancel-queued`
  takes only a job that never started (`REQ-OPERATOR-CONSOLE-ACTIONS`).
- **A cancelled job is never run again, and never recorded against what its requester was told** (issue
  #476, gate of PR #479). The poll runs from pickup, so a cancel could be acknowledged after a job was picked
  up and before the processor handed it back to the queue (one of its holds, the podman.service hold or the
  young-keeper hold, moving it to the delayed set, or any retryable `InfraRetry` failure BullMQ retries after
  its backoff), and the job ran later with its request already consumed; or acknowledged during a
  non-retryable failure, so the requester was told the record would say `operator-cancel` while it said
  `failed`; or acknowledged in the last moment of a run that then recorded its own outcome. So the poll is
  STOPPED by one helper wherever the outcome is decided: at the container's observed exit, as the run returns,
  and in the error handler, before anything is recorded or commented (gate rounds 2 to 4 of PR #479). The stop
  sets a flag the tick reads synchronously right before it aborts and acknowledges, clears the interval, and
  awaits a tick in flight for at most 1 s (`CANCEL_STOP_BOUND_MS`; the worker's Valkey client queues commands
  while offline, so an unbounded wait held the job's record through an outage, and the bound is logged once
  as `cancel_poll_stop_bounded`), so after a stop nothing is acknowledged and an acknowledgement already made
  is on the signal: a read still hanging at the bound returns without acknowledging, and a tick past the flag
  aborted the signal before its ack write. On the success path a cancel acknowledged before the container's exit was seen is the cancel
  (the run takes the aborted path, recorded `operator-cancel`, even if the container exited on its own in the
  same moment, since the requester was told so, and the log names the race); one acknowledged before a
  result with no container (a pre-spend refusal) is recorded as the cancel with the replaced result named in
  the log; one that lands after the stop is never acknowledged, the run keeps its real outcome, and the
  requester's re-read says the job finished. In the error handler the poll is stopped and only then asked. A cancel
  the poll already acknowledged (the signal, aborted with `operator-cancel`) ends the job as that cancel on
  any error, since the requester was told so. A request the poll had not read is read, acknowledged and
  consumed only for a retryable error (the job would otherwise run again), and ends it the same way; for a
  non-retryable error it is left unanswered, so the job fails for its own reason and the requester is told it
  finished. Ending as the cancel means `outcome: "policy", reason: "operator-cancel"`, recorded (it was
  active) with the run's `session` as the aborted-container path keeps it, one fixed comment, never retried:
  a retryable failure that never started says it was cancelled before it started, `budgetReserved: false`;
  one whose container ran keeps its exit, turns, tokens and `budgetReserved: true`, and a non-retryable one
  keeps the `budgetReserved` it carried, both saying the processor's own operator-cancel sentence, the
  non-retryable failure's own words logged beside it. A request landing after the poll stopped is never
  acknowledged, and the requester's timeout re-reads the job's state and says what became of it, each time
  with "nothing was changed": waiting, delayed, prioritized or paused, it went back to the queue before its
  worker read the cancel, so cancel it again to remove it; completed or failed, it finished before its worker
  read the cancel; any other state, it is no longer in the queue. The panel's timeout sentence names these
  cases in one line. A shutdown's abort is not a cancel: that job is held or retried as before, so it
  survives the restart.
  Queued and held cancels write NO run record -- the `dispatch_wait_cancel` rule -- and the CLI says so in its
  output, with the job's past read off BullMQ's `attemptsMade` (issue #477): a job with none never ran; a job with one
  or more (waiting to retry after a failed attempt) made that many attempts, and whatever they recorded stays (no
  record is promised: a gate failing above the processor's `try` counts an attempt and writes none). `removeHeldJob` returns the
  count as `attemptsMade` for the panel's footer. Not `attemptsStarted`, which a hold's `moveToDelayed` increments.
- **Why this is not the Redis state `OQ-008` refuses**: that refusal is about durable CONFIG whose
  deletion silently loses an operator's edit. These keys are transient, attended, TTL-bounded one-shots
  whose loss is REPORTED to an operator watching the ack poll. The falsification test: delete the whole
  `cancel:*` keyspace while the fleet runs, and every job behaves exactly as before the feature existed;
  the only casualty is a pending cancel, whose requester reports the timeout honestly.
- **Residuals, named**: the requester's timeout DEL can lose to a worker GET by one poll tick, so "no
  worker acknowledged" can precede a stop by up to a tick (the message says to re-check `status`); a host
  that is down, a stalled owner, or a worker predating this contract acks nothing and the CLI exits 1
  naming the cause; the record lands up to `ABORT_GRACE_MS` after the ack, because the CLI does not wait
  for the container to die.
- **A sibling channel** (issue #646): `INT-STEER-INBOX-CONTRACT` carries an operator's message INTO a running job the
  way this contract carries a stop, on the same footing: a requester-side CLI verb that resolves the job across the
  fleet's queues (`steer-cli.mjs`, modelled on `cancel-cli.mjs`), transient TTL-bounded keys only a live run's worker
  keeps alive (its open key is refreshed by the job's relay every 2 s, the cadence of this poll), and the same
  falsification test against `OQ-008`. It differs where a message must: its keys are per RUN (`runIdOf`) rather than
  per job id, it has no ack key (the state hash says `written` and `delivered`), and it is opened only for a
  steer-armed attempt. Nothing in this contract changes.

**Code evidence**: worker/src/cancel-state.mjs -> requestCancel, removeHeldJob, and since #737 QUEUED_STATES,
removeQueuedJob, holdInPlace; worker/src/index.mjs -> the cancel poll beside the kill timer, the abortReason mapping;
worker/src/processor.mjs -> the classification; worker/src/cancel-cli.mjs -> runCancel, and since #737 boundedText;
admin/src/read-model.mjs -> cancelHeldJob (delegating); admin/src/job-actions.mjs -> planCancelQueued,
cancelQueuedJob, heldClearedAnswer (since #737); admin/src/dashboard.ts -> cancelActive/cancelHeld deps, the
HELD_LIST view.

## INT-STEER-INBOX-CONTRACT

- **Draft/cancel exception (#766, #772)**: Pre-pickup draft-source refusals use one keeper-free recorder which snapshots project before awaited held/inbox settlement. They close/count late state without resuming paid work. Late-forge callbacks check current draft source before any fallback read/enqueue/post; an unavailable or changed authority releases its semantic window and logs only `steer_late_source_unavailable`. Human and delegated cancellation both suppress late continuation and completed-only collectors, while their request/ack channels and human-touch attribution remain distinct.

**sender (the CLI, or since part 2 the receiver for a forge comment) -> Valkey -> the worker's relay -> `/inbox` (read-only) -> the runner -> pi; and
back: the transcript -> the worker's ack consumer -> Valkey.** The durable inbox of a running, steer-armed job (issue
#646, `REQ-STEER-RUNNING-JOB`, `DES-STEER-VIA-READONLY-INBOX-MOUNT`), the sibling of `INT-CANCEL-CHANNEL-CONTRACT`:
transient, TTL-bounded keys that only a live run's relay keeps alive. One module holds every Valkey side,
`worker/src/steer-inbox.mjs`, exported as `@edgehero/pi-dispatch/steer-inbox` (and the framing as
`@edgehero/pi-dispatch/steer-framing`, and the relay's target derivation as `@edgehero/pi-dispatch/inbox-relay`), so
the CLI, the relay, the settle step, the receiver, the console and the panel cannot drift. Three kinds of sender:
the CLI (`worker/src/steer-cli.mjs`, part 1), the receiver for a forge comment (`receiver/src/steer.mjs`
`trySteer`, part 2, `DES-STEER-TARGET-POINTER-IS-LIVENESS-NOT-INDEX`), which also stores the fallback job, and the
operator console and the `/dispatch` panel (part 3, `planSteer` and `enqueueSteer` in `admin/src/job-actions.mjs`,
`DES-OPERATOR-CONSOLE`); the settle step reads the fallbacks and pre-seeds a resumed job
(`DES-STEER-LATE-MESSAGE-RESUME-OR-REPLY`). `listInboxPublic` is what the console's run page, its state API and the
panel read (part 3): never the text.

- **The run id.** Every key is per RUN: `runIdOf(job)` (`job.data.recoveryOf ?? job.id`, `recovery-queue.mjs`), so
  a #645 recovery and a BullMQ retry find the same inbox; spelled into a key through `sanitizeJobId`, the run
  mirror's sanitizer. A run id is a non-empty string or a non-negative safe integer, else the call is refused.
  **Residual** (part 3 review, named, not fixed here): the sanitizer folds the characters a key must not carry, so
  two run ids that differ only there (`a:b` and `a_b`) share one inbox, as they share the recovery keys; job ids
  minted by this project do not differ that way, and a fix belongs to the run id's spelling everywhere at once.
- **Keys**:
  ```
  run:steer:target:<hex32>     ZSET  member: the raw run id, score: expiresAtMs (refresh time + 30 s); PEXPIRE 60 s.
                                     <hex32> = the first 32 hex of sha256("<kind>\0<repo>\0<targetType>\0<number>"),
                                     number a positive safe integer (a decimal string is accepted), targetType
                                     "pull_request" or "issue". Only a forge job has one; null for a local or cron job.
  run:steer:open:<runId>       STRING the host name (1..255 chars), PX 30 s. The ONE authority on whether a run
                                     takes messages.
  run:inbox:<runId>            LIST   entry JSON, append only (RPUSH), in acceptance order.
  run:inbox:state:<runId>      HASH   <id> -> queued | written | delivered | withdrawn | late, plus `_count` (messages
                                     ever accepted) and `_bytes` (their text bytes), and per message `m:<id>` ->
                                     "<seq> <mode> <source> <at> <bytes>" (part 3, review round 1): its public
                                     metadata, written by the push and the pre-seed in the same script, never text.
  run:inbox:fallback:<runId>   HASH   <id> -> the job JSON a forge message would have started (comment routing;
                                     shape below).
  run:inbox:closed:<runId>     STRING "1", set by the final close.
  steer:steered:<deliveryJobId> STRING "1", EX 31 days, NX: a delivery the receiver steered (part 2 review round 1),
                                     keyed by the job id the comment would have been enqueued under
                                     (`forgeDeliveryJobId`, e.g. `gh-<GUID>`). Written and read by the receiver only.
  ```
- **TTLs** (`STEER_OPEN_TTL_MS` 30 s, `STEER_TARGET_TTL_MS` 60 s, `STEER_INBOX_TTL_MS` 1 h, `STEER_PRESEED_TTL_MS`
  24 h). The list and the state hash get an hour at every accepted push; `storeFallback` gives the fallback hash an
  hour; `registerLive` and its 2 s refresh renew the hour on the list, the state and the fallback hash; the close sets
  `closed` with an hour and gives the list and the state an hour from then. A pre-seed (below) gives the list and the
  state a day, because the run it fills has not started and may wait in the queue; that run's first refresh puts the
  hour back. At the relay's stop the open key and the target member are HELD for `STEER_HOLD_TTL_MS` (15 min,
  `holdLive`, below) until the close removes them. A crashed worker therefore leaves nothing past an hour (a day for a
  pre-seeded run that never started), a running run nothing past 30 s of liveness after its relay goes quiet, and a
  stopped one nothing past 15 minutes. The steered marker lives 31 days.
- **The entry** (`normalizeSteerEntry`; only these fields are kept, rebuilt, never the caller's object):
  ```
  { "v": 1, "id": "<32 lowercase hex>", "mode": "steer" | "followUp",
    "source": "forge" | "console" | "cli" | "panel",
    "author": { "kind": "forge", "id": <forge user id, FORGE_USER_RE>, "association": "<[A-Z][A-Z_]{0,39}>" }
            | { "kind": "operator", "by": "<TOKEN_NAME_RE: [a-z0-9][a-z0-9._-]{0,31}>" },
    "text": "<scrubbed, 1..8192 bytes>", "at": <ms>,
    "deliveryId"?: "<[A-Za-z0-9._:-]{1,128}>", "hop"?: <0..8> }
  ```
  The source and the author must agree: a `forge` source has a forge author, every other source an operator one. The
  CLI writes `source: "cli"`, `author: { kind: "operator", by: "cli" }`; the console (part 3) `source: "console"`,
  `author: { kind: "operator", by: <the session's token name> }`; the panel `source: "panel"`, `author: { kind:
  "operator", by: "panel" }`. `at` defaults to the caller's clock.
  A forge user id (`FORGE_USER_RE`, `worker/src/steer-framing.mjs`, part 2) is a positive integer of up to 15 digits
  (GitHub, GitLab, Forgejo), kept as a number, or an Azure DevOps actor id kept as the string it is: the actor's GUID
  (`8-4-4-4-12` hex, either case), or `azid-` and 16 lowercase hex, the first 16 of `sha256(address)`, which the
  Azure filter derives when the event names the actor only by address (`stableActorId`; `INT-AZURE-PAYLOAD-SUBSET`
  is unchanged by this). Every form is charset-safe, so the attribution line never carries a sender's text. The
  receiver writes `source: "forge"`, `mode` from the filter's `steerMode`, `deliveryId` the delivery's, and `author`
  `{ kind: "forge", id: <sender id>, association }`, where the association is the comment's `author_association`
  on GitHub and the fixed word `WRITE_ACCESS` (`FORGE_GATE_ASSOCIATION`) on GitLab, Forgejo and Azure DevOps, whose
  gate is the receiver's resolved write-access verdict rather than a role it could name. An entry the framing could
  not frame with the longest ref (`STEER_REF_WORST`) is refused at normalisation, so a message is never accepted that
  the relay would then have to refuse.
- **Ids.** A forge message's id is the first 32 hex of `sha256("forge\0" + deliveryId)` (`forgeMessageId`), so a
  redelivered webhook GUID is the same message and pushes `dup`; an operator message's is 16 random bytes in hex
  (`operatorMessageId`). The same delivery in two runs' inboxes (a fanout to replicas) has the same id in each.
- **The fallback job** (`storeFallback`, `readFallbacks`; part 2). `run:inbox:fallback:<runId>` maps a forge
  message's id to the JSON of the job the receiver would have enqueued for that comment had no run been live: the
  filter's job object without `steerMode`, plus `kind` (the forge) and `jobId` (its delivery job id,
  `forgeDeliveryJobId`, or null). `enqueueLateForgeJob` rebuilds the job from it through `enqueueForgeJob`'s explicit
  field list, so a field outside that list never reaches a queue; the stored `jobId` is informational and the id is
  recomputed from `trigger.deliveryId`. The receiver stores it for each live run BEFORE that run's push
  (`DES-STEER-TARGET-POINTER-IS-LIVENESS-NOT-INDEX`), so a store whose push is then refused leaves an orphan that
  nothing reads and the hour removes. `readFallbacks` answers `{ jobs: { id: job } }`, dropping a field whose name is
  not a message id or whose value does not parse as an object. It holds the comment's text (inside `trigger`), like
  the queued job it stands for; it is read only by the settle step. The store is one script (`FALLBACK`, review round
  1; KEYS fallback; ARGV id, job JSON, max, ttl): refused `full` when the id is new and the hash already holds
  `STEER_MAX_FALLBACKS` (32, twice the message cap, because a store precedes a push the run may refuse), else HSET
  (a redelivered id overwrites its entry and is never counted) and the hour. `storeFallback` answers `{ ok: true }`,
  `{ error: "full" }` or `{ error }`; the receiver then skips that run's push.
- **Caps** (`STEER_MAX_MESSAGES` 16, `STEER_TOTAL_MAX_BYTES` 65,536, `STEER_TEXT_MAX_BYTES` 8,192 per message, the
  console answer's own bound, `ANSWER_TEXT_MAX_BYTES`). The text is scrubbed by `scrubSteerText`: first
  `console-answer.mjs`'s `scrubAnswerText` (CR and CRLF to LF, U+2028 and U+2029 to LF, a tab to a space, every other
  C0 and C1 control and the bidi controls removed), then the characters a model reads and a reviewer does not see are
  removed (the Unicode tag block U+E0000 to U+E007F, U+200B to U+200D, U+2060 to U+2064, U+180E and U+FEFF; an emoji
  joined with U+200D arrives as its separate emoji), and three backtick look-alikes (U+FF40, U+02CB, U+1FEF) become
  the ASCII backtick, so `fenceBlock` counts them in the run it must out-length. Nothing else is normalised: NFKC is
  deliberately not applied, because it rewrites far more than look-alikes (a CJK writer's fullwidth punctuation,
  ligatures, superscripts) and can lengthen a text past the cap it was measured under (U+FDFA becomes eighteen code
  points), while the framing promises the message verbatim and the fence is defense in depth. A text holding an
  unpaired UTF-16 surrogate is refused, never replaced with U+FFFD. The extra scrub lives on the steer path only:
  `scrubAnswerText`'s output is quoted on the forge by a parked answer's trail comment, where U+200B is the mention
  neutraliser. The scrubbed text is then bounded by `boundAnswerText`'s decision, refused in this feature's words,
  NEVER cut: a truncated message is one the person did not send. A message whose inbox file would exceed 16 KiB, measured with
  the longest possible ref (`STEER_REF_WORST`), is refused at push too, since once accepted it could never be written.
  The count and byte caps are enforced inside the push script, so concurrent pushers cannot race past them, and
  count every message ever accepted, withdrawn ones included, so withdraw and push again cannot flood a run.
- **The scripts.** Every state change is one Lua script, a compare and set against the state hash run atomically by
  Valkey:
  - `PUSH` (KEYS open, closed, list, state; ARGV id, entry JSON, text bytes, max count, max bytes, ttl) returns, in
    this order of checks, `dup` (the id is already in the state hash, whatever became of the run since: a redelivered
    GUID must not enqueue its fallback twice), `closed` (the closed key exists; checked before `gone` because the
    close deletes the open key too and "finished" is the truer answer), `gone` (no open key), `full` (one more would
    pass a cap), else RPUSHes the entry, sets the id `queued`, adds to `_count` and `_bytes`, refreshes the hour, and
    returns `ok`. `pushSteer` answers one of those five words, `{ error: "refused", reason }` for an entry refused
    before Valkey is touched, or `{ error: <code> }`.
  - `WITHDRAW` (KEYS state; ARGV id): `queued` or `written` becomes `withdrawn`, anything else is left; returns the
    state it found, nil when the id is unknown. `withdrawSteer` answers `{ prior }`: `queued` is a GUARANTEED
    withdrawal (the relay never wrote it), `written` best effort (the runner may have read the file before the relay
    unlinks it), `prior: null` no such message.
  - `CLOSE` (KEYS closed, open, list, state, and the target when the run has one; ARGV the raw run id, ttl): sets
    `closed` (PX the ttl), DELs the open key, ZREMs the run from its target, turns every `queued` or `written` id
    into `late`, refreshes the list's and the state's hour, and returns `[list, state, first]`, `first` 1 only when
    the closed key did not exist before this call (review round 1). `closeInbox` answers
    `{ entries, state, count, bytes, first }`; a second close of the same run (a terminal thrown failure is settled by
    the processor and then by the failed listener) gets the same entries with `first: false`, and only the first may
    answer or resume them. After it every push is refused, and everything pushed before it is in its
    reply. Called only by the settle step, at a final outcome (`DES-STEER-LATE-MESSAGE-RESUME-OR-REPLY`).
  - `MARK` (KEYS state; ARGV id, to, from...): moves the id to `to` only when it is in one of `from`; returns
    `{1, prior}` or `{0, prior}`. `markState` answers `{ ok, prior }`. The relay's moves: `queued` to `written`
    before the rename; `written`, `queued` or `withdrawn` to `delivered` on a verified ack (a written message withdrawn
    best effort that the agent did receive is delivered); `delivered` to `written` at a re-baseline; the waiting
    state to `late` for an entry the framing refuses.
  - Liveness (`registerLive`, `refreshLive`): one `MULTI` that SETs the open key PX 30 s and, for a forge job,
    ZREMRANGEBYSCOREs the target's members whose score has passed, ZADDs the run at `now + 30 s` and PEXPIREs the
    target 60 s, then refreshes the list's, the state's and the fallback hash's hour.
  - `HOLD` (`holdLive`, the relay's stop since part 2 review round 1; KEYS closed, open, and the target when the run has
    one; ARGV host, now ms, hold ms, the raw run id): nothing (returns 0) when the closed key exists; else SETs the
    open key PX the hold, ZADDs the run at `now + hold`, raises the target's PTTL to the hold when it is shorter (never
    lowers it), and returns 1. `holdLive` answers `{ held }` or `{ error }`. Not a close: a retry or a recovery finds
    the inbox open, and a message pushed meanwhile is written by the next attempt or closed `late`. The hold is
    `STEER_HOLD_TTL_MS`, 15 minutes, longer than the semantic window. **Residual**: a later `registerLive` by another
    run on the same target sets the target's TTL back to 60 s, so a held member can expire with the key early if that
    run then stops refreshing without a hold. `unregisterLive` (DEL the open key, ZREM the member, not a close) is
    kept for a caller that must make a run unreachable at once; the relay no longer calls it.
  - `PRESEED` (`preseedInbox`, part 2; KEYS closed, list, state; ARGV ttl, max count, max bytes, then id, entry
    JSON, text bytes per message): fills the inbox of a run that has NOT STARTED (a late message's resumed job,
    keyed by its new job id) with carried messages. No open-key check (no relay has registered it), but every other
    rule of a push: `closed` when the closed key exists, a message whose id is already in the state hash skipped,
    the two caps judged for the batch as a whole, all or nothing (`full`), before anything is written; then each new
    entry RPUSHed and set `queued`, `_count` and `_bytes` raised, and the list and the state given
    `STEER_PRESEED_TTL_MS`. `preseedInbox` takes 1 to 16 entries, each validated as a push validates it and each
    required to carry `hop >= 1` (a carried message is never a first one; one carried that turns late again is
    answered, never carried a second time), dedups repeated ids in the batch, and answers `{ seeded: n }` (n new),
    `{ error: "closed" | "full" }`, a refusal, or `{ error: <code> }`. Worker only: no surface takes a message for a
    run that is not live through it.
  - `RESET` (the relay's `start`, `resetClosedInbox`, review round 1; KEYS list, state, fallback, closed): when the
    closed key exists, DELs all four and returns 1, else returns 0 and touches nothing. It runs BEFORE `registerLive`,
    so no push can be accepted into the old run's keys. It exists for a run that reuses a run id whose run already
    ended: a console retry of a failed job keeps its job id, so its run id, and found the previous run's closed inbox
    (every push `closed` for an hour, and the re-baseline handing that run's delivered messages to a run never sent
    them). The previous run's outcome is already recorded, since the close precedes the record write. An OPEN inbox (a
    #645 recovery, an `InfraRetry` with attempts left) is never reset: those attempts continue the same run. A reset
    is logged `steer_inbox_reset`; a failed one is a relay fault (`reset`), and the relay then reads the inbox as
    closed on every tick, so it never writes into it nor re-baselines it (`steer_inbox_closed`, said once).
  - Reads: `readInbox` (LRANGE, HGETALL, EXISTS closed in one MULTI; text included, for the relay only),
    `listInboxPublic` (`{ entries: [{ id, mode, source, state, at, bytes }], closed }`, NEVER the text, read from
    the state hash's `m:<id>` fields in `seq` order with one HGETALL and one EXISTS, so the list and its text are
    not moved; a message held without its field, from a worker before part 3, falls back to reading the list),
    `messageState` (one HGET, the CLI's poll), `isOpen` (EXISTS on the open key), `liveRunsForTarget`
    (`ZRANGEBYSCORE target (now +inf LIMIT 0 n`, n 4 by default and at most 64). A list line that does not parse as an
    entry with a valid id is dropped, never surfaced as text.
  - **Never throws.** Every export answers a value or `{ error }`: a validation refusal is `{ error: "refused",
    reason }` with an operator-readable reason, a Valkey fault `{ error: <code> }` naming no key or value. A caller
    must fail loudly on either and never read it as an empty inbox.
- **The inbox file** (the relay, `worker/src/inbox-relay.mjs`; the runner, `image/runner/src/inbox.mjs`). The host
  directory is `<jobDir>.inbox`, beside the job directory and never inside it, mode 0700, made fresh per attempt and
  removed when the attempt ends, mounted at `/inbox` read-only (`INT-CONTAINER-JOB-INPUTS`). A message's file is
  written as `.<id>.tmp` with mode 0444 (`flag: "wx"`, an old temporary file removed first), and renamed to
  `<seq>-<id>.json`, where `<seq>` is the entry's 1-based position in the list, six digits, zero padded
  (`inboxFileName`), only after the `queued` to `written` mark succeeded. Its body is exactly
  `{"v":1,"id":"<id>","mode":"<mode>","source":"<source>","content":"<framed text>"}` (`steerFileJson`), at most
  16 KiB. The runner reads only names matching `^\d{6}-([0-9a-f]{32})\.json$`, in name order, refuses (once, logged by
  id and reason, `steer_file_refused`) a file over 16 KiB, one that is not a JSON object, one with any other key, a
  `v` other than 1, an id that is not the name's, a mode or source outside the lists, or an empty content; a file
  gone between the listing and the read is skipped and read again if rewritten. It holds what it read in two FIFOs
  by mode, each in name order (issue #670): mid-run it hands over only steers, and at `agent_before_settle` a
  waiting steer first, else the oldest follow-up, one message in flight at a time either way. Just before each push
  it checks the entry's file again: a file the relay unlinked (a message withdrawn while the runner held it) is
  dropped, logged as `steer_withdrawn_held {id, mode, source}` and never handed over, and the close's last read drops
  such an entry too. `content` is the framing (`frameSteerMessage`, `DES-STEER-VIA-READONLY-INBOX-MOUNT`), the text
  inside `fenceBlock`.
- **The ack.** The runner hands a message to pi as `{ customType: "pi-dispatch-inbox", content: [{ type: "text",
  text: <content> }], display: true, details: { id, mode, source, ack } }` with `deliverAs: "steer"` (issue #670:
  mid-run only steers go, and a follow-up is handed over at the settle boundary as a pi steer, `details.mode` still
  `followUp`), where
  `ack = hex(HMAC-SHA256(exitKey, "pi-dispatch-inbox-ack\0" + runId + "\0" + id))`, `exitKey` the per-attempt key the
  worker wrote to the runner's stdin (issue #545) and `runId` the container's `PI_JOB_ID`, which the worker sets to
  the job's CONTAINER name (the venue's name for this attempt's queue job, `pi-job-<queue id>` on the local venue), not to the run id the keys use. The worker's `inboxAck` is the
  runner's restated byte for byte (pinned by a test), and `makeSteerAck` verifies a `custom_message` of that type
  against the same container name (`ackRunId: name`) under the same attempt's key, in constant time; the key is minted
  per attempt, so it is what separates one attempt's acks from another's, and the string only has to match. A line
  that ended at or before the tail's baseline is a PRIOR line: never counted live, its id joins the prior set the relay
  re-baselines against, and when its ack verifies under THIS attempt's key the relay marks a still waiting message
  `delivered` at the baseline instead of writing it again (review round 1, F5).
  **Residual, named (F5)**: a line an EARLIER attempt wrote never verifies here, because that attempt's key is gone.
  So a message delivered just before a crash, whose state is still `written` and whose line is in the restored
  transcript, is handed over a second time by the recovery (a duplicate, framed, never a loss). Unverified prior lines
  are deliberately not trusted: the transcript is agent-writable, and trusting them would let the agent mark a message
  delivered that it was never sent by planting a line in a transcript a recovery restores.
  **The signed exit line is a second witness** (review round 1, F3). The runner's exit line carries `steer.deliveredIds`
  (`INT-RUNNER-EXIT-CODE-PROTOCOL`): the ids it saw pi persist, at most 16. When the exit line VERIFIED under the
  attempt's exit key, `runContainer` first drains the transcript acks in flight, then marks each of those ids
  `delivered` through the relay, and only then stops the relay; an unverified line marks nothing. So an agent that
  breaks the transcript (a symlink swapped in at `/session/current.jsonl` makes the tail refuse the file) can no
  longer make delivered messages settle as `late`.
- **A second transport: stdin frames (copying venues). AMENDED 2026-10-18 (issue #680), built in #686. AMENDED
  2026-10-19 (issue #686 part 2): SHIPPED on `openshell`, the names final, written from `worker/src/steer-framing.mjs`
  (`encodeFrame`, `keyFrame`, `frameMac`, `steerFrame`, `STEER_STDIN_BUDGET_BYTES`), `worker/src/inbox-relay.mjs`
  (`frames`, `attach`), `worker/src/run-container.mjs`, `image/runner/src/steer-frames.mjs`,
  `image/runner/src/supervise.mjs` and `image/runner/src/inbox.mjs`; "as built" below names what the text
  before it did not.** The `/inbox` mount above needs a venue that binds: a venue that uploads `/job` once
  cannot show the runner a file written later, which is why such a venue is skipped today (`steerSkipped:
  "venue-copies"`). On a COPYING venue (the first is `openshell` in its default copy mode, `DES-OPENSHELL-VENUE`; its
  opt-in bind mode, #686, binds and takes the mount) the relay instead writes each message as a frame on the main
  exec's stdin, the pipe issue #545 already uses for the exit key (`INT-RUNNER-EXIT-CODE-PROTOCOL`, AMENDED the same
  day). Everything above the inbox file (the keys, the scripts, the caps, the ids, the framing of the text, the ack,
  the exit line's `deliveredIds`, the record) is the same on both transports; this bullet defines only what replaces
  the file.
  - **Arming.** An attempt is stdin-steered when the job asks (`job.steer === true`), the venue copies, the image
    declares `exitAuth` and the capability **`steerStdin`** (the runner reads frames, and `verify-image.sh`
    proves the two process properties below), and a transcript tail and a relay exist. As built: the transcript tail
    is the stdio transcript over the exec's stderr (`INT-RUNNER-EXIT-CODE-PROTOCOL`'s transcript records, armed by
    `transcriptStderr`), where the acks come back; an attempt that has every other part but not that one is
    `steerSkipped: "no-transcript"`, as a binding venue without a tail is. No new skip reason. An
    image without `steerStdin` on a copying venue is skipped exactly as today, `steerSkipped: "venue-copies"`, and the
    job runs unsteered: `steerStdin` is a capability token, not a pre-spend gate, because a job on a copying venue
    already runs without steering when it cannot be armed, and the record says why. A bind venue never uses this
    transport, whatever the image declares.
  - **The frame.** A 4-byte big-endian unsigned length, then exactly that many bytes of UTF-8 JSON, one object.
    **Frame 1 is the exit key**, `{"t":"key","key":"<64 lowercase hex>"}`, written at the spawn and read by the
    in-image supervisor and the runner before pi loads, so no tool exists while it is in the pipe (#545's property). **Every
    later frame is one message**:
    `{"t":"steer","seq":<n>,"v":1,"id":"<id>","mode":"<mode>","source":"<source>","content":"<framed text>","mac":"<64 hex>"}`,
    `v`, `id`, `mode` (`steer` or `followUp`), `source` and `content` exactly the inbox file's fields and values
    (`steerFileJson`'s), `seq` the frame's position in this attempt's stream (the key frame is 1, so the first message
    is 2), and
    `mac = hex(HMAC-SHA256(exitKey, "pi-dispatch-inbox-frame\0" + runId + "\0" + seq + "\0" + body))`, where `exitKey`
    and `runId` are the ack's (the per-attempt key, and `PI_JOB_ID`, the name the venue gives this attempt), `seq` is
    written in decimal, and `body` is the exact bytes `steerFileJson` writes for those five fields, so the MAC covers
    the id, the mode, the source and the content, and a frame cannot be re-labelled from a steer to a follow-up. The
    domain string differs from the ack's `pi-dispatch-inbox-ack\0`, and the input from the exit line's, so an ack the
    agent reads in its transcript, or the exit line, is never a valid frame MAC. The runner applies every refusal the
    file has (any other key, a `v` other than 1, a mode or source outside the lists, an empty content, a body over
    16 KiB) and accepts a verified frame only when its id is unseen this attempt and its `seq` is above the last
    accepted; it then holds and hands it over exactly as a file's message (two FIFOs by mode, the ack, the exit
    line's counts).
  - **The budget.** At most 4 MiB (4,194,304 bytes) in total over the attempt, every frame counted with its 4-byte
    prefix, the key frame included: the stdin buffer OpenShell's exec path holds, as #686 reads it at the pin; if
    that measurement is smaller, the cap moves down, never up. The relay counts what it wrote and refuses a frame
    larger than the remaining budget: the message is not written, its state moves to `late` as for an entry the
    framing refuses (`MARK`, `steer_frame_refused {jobId, id}`), and a message is never cut. The inbox's own caps
    (16 messages, 64 KiB of text) keep a run far below it; the cap exists so a pipe the venue buffers is never asked
    to hold more than it can. **As #686 reads it at the pin (MEASURED, OpenShell 0.1.4, `.github/openshell.json`)**:
    piped stdin over 4 MiB in total makes the exec exit 1 with "streamed stdin exceeds the 4 MiB limit", and 4 MiB
    minus 1 KiB passed; so the cap stands at 4 MiB, and the relay's budget (`STEER_STDIN_BUDGET_BYTES`, the runner's
    copy pinned to it by `worker/test/steer-frames.test.mjs`) sits at 4,193,280 bytes, the largest total the lab saw
    pass, because exactly 4 MiB was not measured and the CLI's own accounting of its stream is its code. The runner
    holds a declared length past what is left of the same budget to be a `length` break.
  - **What breaks the stream.** A declared length the relay could never have written (zero, over the remaining
    budget, or over the 16 KiB body plus the frame's extra keys, as built `STEER_FRAME_MAX_BYTES`, 16 KiB + 256; and,
    as built, a frame EOF cuts), bytes that are not UTF-8 JSON, an object that is
    neither shape, or a key-shaped frame (`"t":"key"`) after frame 1, which is a `shape` break and never a re-key (the
    runner accepts exactly one key per attempt, frame 1's): the runner stops reading steer frames for the attempt, logs `steer_stream_broken {reason}` (a fixed
    token: `length`, `json`, `shape`), and every message not yet accepted settles undelivered. A well-formed frame
    whose MAC does not verify is dropped and reading goes on; drops are counted and logged once per attempt,
    `steer_frame_unverified {count}`, by that fixed token and a number, never the frame's text or id. The names are
    final. As built: the runner logs `steer_frame_unverified` once, at the inbox's close, with the attempt's count; a
    verified frame whose `seq` is not above the last accepted or whose id is already seen (a replay, or an id the
    transcript's seed shows delivered) is dropped silently, since it is a genuine message already held; a verified
    frame the file's refusals refuse is logged as the file's `steer_file_refused {id, reason}`, the same reasons.
  - **Close.** The relay closes the pipe when it withdraws the attempt's arming (its stop) or when the attempt ends;
    the runner reads EOF as no more messages and keeps what it already holds. A `WITHDRAW` of a `written` message is
    weaker here than on the mount: there is no file to unlink, so a frame already in the pipe is still handed over,
    and its verified ack moves it from `withdrawn` to `delivered` as `MARK` already does; a `queued` withdrawal stays
    guaranteed, since the relay never wrote it. As built: the relay marks `queued` to `written` BEFORE it writes the
    frame (the file's mark-before-rename), waits out the pipe's backpressure (`drain`) one frame at a time, and ends
    the pipe at its stop, which `runContainer` calls once the exec has closed; a write error on the pipe (EPIPE) is
    caught on the stream and logged once as `steer_relay_fault {jobId, step: "stdin", code}`, never thrown. **And
    earlier, at the exit line** (review round 1, M1, a defence: OpenShell 0.1.4's CLI exits with its stdin still open,
    measured on the real gateway): `runContainer` ends the pipe (`closeStdin`, the relay running on for the acks) as
    soon as a line on the exec's stdout VERIFIES as the attempt's exit line, or `stdinExitGraceMs` (5 s) after an
    exit-shaped line that does not (the supervisor's unkeyed line, a forgery), so a CLI that waited for EOF could never
    deadlock on the relay and a forged line can only end steering early. Nothing the runner would read is lost: it
    has closed its inbox before its exit line. The close is logged once, `steer_stdin_closed {container, reason}`
    (`exit-verified` or `exit-unverified`), and a message accepted after it is never written and settles `late` at the
    close of the inbox, as one the run never took. **No pass before `start`** (review round 1, L6): the relay runs no
    pass until its start has reset a closed inbox and registered the run, and then runs the one a baseline that came
    first asked for, so the release at the spawn below can never read or write the previous run's closed inbox. **The
    baseline as built**: the relay writes nothing before the ack consumer's baseline (`onBaseline`, the stdio
    transcript's, which waits for the runner's signed baseline record), EXCEPT that an attempt with no staged
    transcript (not a resume, not a recovery) is released at the spawn, since the upload is the preparer's empty live
    file and holds no prior line: a message queued before the start then reaches the runner before its first
    `agent_start`, where pi polls steering once before the first model call, instead of racing the run (measured on
    Docker under a cost cap of 0: the record came back about 600 ms in, the run was over at about 700). The runner
    holds a frame read before its session exists and drops it at the seed when the transcript already delivered it.
  - **The residual, stated plainly: this transport is weaker than the read-only `/inbox` mount, which is why bind
    venues keep the mount.** The agent runs as the runner's uid, and on Linux the design assumes it can open the pipe
    for READ and WRITE through a holder's `/proc/<pid>/fd/0` (the runner's own is refused by the exec-only node;
    another holder's need not be, and how OpenShell's exec hands the pipe in is its code, not ours). It **cannot
    plant** a message: the key left the pipe before any tool existed, and a frame without a valid MAC is dropped. It
    **can consume** one, which WITHDRAWS it: the runner never sees it, no ack arrives, and the worker reports it
    undelivered exactly as today, `late` at the close (`settleInbox`). A frame it reads and writes back is the
    genuine frame again, accepted once by its id and `seq`, so the agent can delay or drop a message and can break
    the stream (which drops every later one), never forge, duplicate, re-label or reorder one. Under the mount it can
    do none of these: the kernel refuses its write and the relay owns the directory. A delivery is still confirmed
    only by the ack under the exit key, so a withdrawal is never reported as a delivery; what is lost is the
    guarantee that a sent message reaches the agent at all.
  - **No TTY and no other channel.** The exec is started without a terminal, and the runner gives every tool child
    `/dev/null` as stdin, so a `bash` call cannot read a frame by inheriting fd 0; `verify-image.sh` proves both on an
    image declaring `steerStdin` (#686). The container gains no network path, credential or listening socket. As
    built (`INT-RUNNER-EXIT-CODE-PROTOCOL`'s "As built"): the frames reach the runner on its fd 3, which no tool child
    inherits, and its fd 0 is `/dev/null` from before any extension loads; `verify-image.sh` reads fd 0 from pi's own
    bash tool operations (`createLocalBashOperations`) and from a child spawned with inherited stdin, both
    `/dev/null`.
- **Who writes what.** The open key, the target member and the inbox's hour: the relay of an armed attempt alone,
  from the container's start until it stops, when it holds the open key and the member for 15 minutes (`HOLD`). The entries: the senders, through `PUSH`, and the settle step, through
  `PRESEED`, into a resumed job's inbox. The fallback hash: the receiver (`storeFallback`). The states: `PUSH` and
  `PRESEED` (`queued`), the relay (`written`; `delivered` off a verified transcript ack, a verified prior line or a verified exit
  line's id; `late` for an unframable entry; `written` again at a re-baseline), `WITHDRAW` (`withdrawn`) and `CLOSE`
  (`late`). `RESET` deletes a closed inbox's keys at a new run's start. Nothing in the container touches Valkey.
- **The record.** At the final outcome the settle step counts the closed states into the record's `steered:
  { delivered, late, withdrawn }`, and the attempt's arming verdict is `steerSkipped` (`venue-copies`,
  `no-exit-key`, `no-transcript`, `no-inbox`), both only for a job whose data says `steer: true`
  (`INT-RUN-HISTORY-FILE-CONTRACT`). The close runs before every record write of a final outcome, and also from the
  failed listener's terminal branch (review round 1, F2), so a terminal failure the processor never saw (a stall-kill
  of a crashed worker's job, a rethrow above its catch) closes the inbox and its waiting messages count `late`
  instead of sitting `queued` until the key expires. The runner's own counts ride its exit line as `steer: {
  delivered, pending, deliveredIds }` (`INT-RUNNER-EXIT-CODE-PROTOCOL`), `pending` being the steers and the
  follow-ups it holds plus the one in flight, a message withdrawn while held never among them (issue #670; on the
  SIGTERM line too, which closes the inbox before it counts, as the decided line's close does);
  `runContainer`'s result keeps only `{ delivered, pending }`.
- **Why this is not the Redis state `OQ-008` refuses**, `INT-CANCEL-CHANNEL-CONTRACT`'s argument: these are
  transient, TTL-bounded keys of a live run, not durable configuration. Delete the whole `run:steer:*` and
  `run:inbox:*` keyspace while the fleet runs and every job behaves as before; the casualties are the messages in
  flight, and a sender is told (`gone`, or `late` at its next read). Why the target pointer is not a session index is
  `DES-STEER-TARGET-POINTER-IS-LIVENESS-NOT-INDEX`. The steered marker (`steer:steered:*`) is the one key here that
  outlives a run: it is the delivery-GUID shield's stand-in for a comment that was never enqueued, the same class and
  the same 31-day retention as the BullMQ job hash that shield rests on (`REQ-DEDUP-BY-DELIVERY-GUID`), holding
  nothing but `1`. Deleting it loses exactly that shield: a later redelivery of a steered comment would start a job.
- **The receiver's answer** (part 2). A webhook delivery whose comment at least one live run took (`ok` or `dup`)
  is answered `202 {"status":"steered","runs":<n>}`, n the runs that took it, and nothing is enqueued; after such a
  steer the receiver sets the steered marker (after the push, never before). One no run took, after a successful
  live-run lookup, is checked against the marker: present (a redelivery of a delivery steered before, whose run has
  ended), it is answered `202 {"status":"steered","runs":0}` and never enqueued (review round 1). Otherwise it is
  enqueued and answered exactly as before (`202` queued or deduplicated, `202` held since issue #638 (the next bullet), `503` on an enqueue fault); a lookup fault,
  or a fanout in which every store or push errored, falls through without the marker check. The poller has no answer
  to give: a marked redelivery is neither enqueued nor counted, and its `poll_cycle` line gains `steered: <n>` only
  in a cycle where a comment steered. The target key's repo is the job's own spelling, for the poller its
  `POLL_REPOS` entry's, which is what the poller's runs registered under; a deployment serving one repository by
  both webhook and poller with a differently cased entry keys the two apart (its comments fall through to ordinary
  jobs), and the two transports see one comment under different delivery ids (the old residual: it can be handled
  twice).
- **Held replies: a sibling key set, not the inbox** (issue #638, `DES-AWAIT-INPUT-ENDS-THE-JOB`). One module,
  `worker/src/held-replies.mjs`, exported as `@edgehero/pi-dispatch/held-replies`; the worker's keeper and settle are
  `worker/src/held-settle.mjs`, the receiver's side `receiver/src/held.mjs`. Per RUN, spelled like the inbox's keys:
  ```
  run:await:target:<hex32>     ZSET  member: the raw run id, score: expiresAtMs (refresh time + 30 s); PEXPIRE 60 s.
                                     <hex32> is the steer target's own hash (`awaitTargetKeyOf` cuts it off the
                                     `steerTargetOf` key, never re-spells it). Every job with `awaitInput: true` and a
                                     forge target, steer-armed or not.
  run:await:open:<runId>       STRING the host name, PX 30 s: the ONE authority on whether a run takes a held reply.
  run:held:<runId>             LIST  entry JSON {"id","at","route","fallback"} in that order, append only, PEXPIRE 1 h;
                                     id the 32-hex `forgeMessageId` of the delivery; route "dedup" | "pre-label";
                                     fallback the job the receiver would have enqueued (`fallbackJobOf`, the inbox
                                     fallback's shape: the filter's job without `steerMode`, plus `kind` and `jobId`).
  run:held:closed:<runId>      STRING "1", PX 1 h, set by the settle's close.
  run:await:parked:<hex32>     STRING the run id, PX 60 s, set by the park's close in the same script: a run parked
                                     here a moment ago (review round 2). Read by the receiver only.
  ```
  Never under `run:steer:*` or `run:inbox:*`: `trySteer` never sees an awaitInput run, and a held reply is never a
  steer. **Who writes**: the processor's keeper registers the run once the pickup's gates (pause, size, wait, scope,
  endpoint, host slot) have admitted it, just before the settings overlay check and `runJob` (one MULTI: open key,
  target member, the list's hour), and refreshes it every 2 s until the park's take or the final settle stops it; its start first
  resets a CLOSED list of the same run id (`RESET`, a console retry keeps the job id); its stop deletes nothing. **The
  scripts**: `HOLD` (KEYS open, closed, list; ARGV the id's JSON prefix, entry JSON, max 20, ttl) returns `closed`,
  `gone`, `dup` (an entry with that id is listed) or `ok` in that order of checks, and at 20 entries evicts the
  oldest (`LTRIM`) rather than refusing; an entry over 1 MiB is refused before Valkey. `CLOSE` (KEYS closed, open,
  list, the target, and for the park's take the parked marker; ARGV the raw run id, ttl, the marker's ttl) sets
  `closed`, drops the open key and the target member, raises the marker when given, and returns `[list, first]`, `first` 1 only for the call that
  closed it. **The receiver's answer**: a delivery a live run held (`ok` or `dup`) and that created no job is answered
  `202 {"status":"held","runs":<n>}`. Two routes: a comment-matched job with `resume` and `awaitInput` that the
  semantic window deduplicated is held under each surviving job id (the swallow is still logged `deduplicated`); a
  filter drop carrying `heldCandidate` (a phrase-free reply on an issue lacking only the parked marker) is held under
  every live run on the await target, at most 4; when no live run takes it but the target's parked marker stands, it
  is enqueued as the parked reply it is (logged `held_after_park`, answered as any enqueue). A hold no run took is
  answered exactly as before (`202` deduplicated, or `204` with today's `dropped` line). The poller holds by the same two routes and counts `held: <n>`
  on its `poll_cycle` line only in a cycle that held one. **The take** (`takeHeld`, inside the processor's park
  sequence: promote, marker on, release the window, take, comment) acts on the first close only: entries whose `at`
  is more than `HELD_LOOKBACK_MS` (5 min) before the take are dropped; the first remaining entry whose fallback names
  the run's forge, repo, target type and number, flow and command (a mismatch is skipped for the next) is enqueued WITH the semantic
  window (`enqueueForgeJob`) on the queue that ran the run; an add the window swallows is not taken; the rest get one
  `HELD_EXTRA_REPLY` (or one `HELD_RESUME_FAILED_REPLY` when nothing could be started, also for a close that failed);
  and the processor posts `HELD_TAKEN_COMMENT` instead of the parked comment when one was taken, here or (`taken:
  "other"`) by another job the window showed already holds the answer; the take's close also raises the parked
  marker. **The settle** (at a
  final outcome, `isFinalOutcome`, the inbox settle's three sites) is the backstop: after a take it finds the list
  closed and does nothing; after a take whose own close failed it only drops; for any outcome that is not a park it
  drops every held reply. **Logs**, ids and counts
  only: the receiver's and the poller's `held {delivery, repo, target, route, runId}` and `held_fell_through
  {delivery, kind, route, reason, outcomes?}`; the keeper's `held_keeper_fault {jobId, step, code}`; the settle's
  `held_reply_resumed {jobId, runId, n, queue}`, `held_replies_dropped {runId, n, stale?}`, `held_reply_mismatch
  {runId}`, `held_reply_not_taken {runId, survivingJobId}`, `held_reply_resume_failed {runId, queue, code}` and `held_settle_failed {jobId, code}`. Like the inbox keys these
  are transient, TTL-bounded keys of a live run (`OQ-008` does not apply): delete them and every reply is answered as
  it was before this feature.
- **Logs** carry the job id, message ids, step names, codes and counts, never a message's text: the relay's
  `steer_relay_fault {jobId, step, code}` (once per step and code), `steer_frame_refused {jobId, id}`,
  `steer_inbox_reset {jobId}` and `steer_inbox_closed {jobId}` (once); the ack
  consumer's `steer_ack_unverified {jobId, id?}` (once per attempt); the settle step's `steer_settled_late`,

## INT-ON-FAILURE-HOOK-CONTRACT

**Producer**: the worker's two terminal listeners (start.mjs). **Consumer**: ONE operator-named command
(`PI_ON_FAILURE`, absolute path, boot-refused otherwise; issue #288). The operator wires the transport;
this project never grows one.

- **Invocation**: the worker spawns the named path with id-only argv --
  `<jobId> <outcome> <reason> <host>` -- never a title, a body, or any payload text
  (`CONST-ISSUE-TEXT-IS-DATA`). `shell: false`, an argv array, ALL THREE stdio streams `ignore` --
  nothing is entitled to read a notification's output, which is one subtraction beyond the wait check's
  byte counters, and with no pipes the backgrounded-grandchild EOF hazard cannot arise (the listener is
  still `exit`). It runs on the HOST as the worker, with the worker's environment: this is not a weaker
  blast radius than `--env-setup`, it is the same one at a different time, and what bounds it is that
  the operator named the script in a file only they can write.
- **The reason is shape-guarded at the spawn**, the single normalizing door: a value that is not a record reason
  token (`RECORD_REASON_RE`, `^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{0,63}$`, the run record's own rule from the worker's leaf
  `record-reason.mjs`; AMENDED 2026-10-26, #737 PR 4a, where it was `^[a-z0-9-]{1,40}$`, which flattened a reason of
  41 to 64 characters that the record keeps to `infra`) flattens to `infra` before it can become argv, because
  `InfraRetry.reason` defaults to the whole message when no token was given and messages carry library words. Argv[1..3]
  must be non-empty and no element may lead with a dash; `host` may honestly be `""`. **AMENDED 2026-10-26 (#737,
  PR 4a)**: the terminal failed listener passes the thrown error's `reason`, and the container's two exits now throw
  with tokens of their own, so a final failure on the runner's infrastructure exit (code 1) crosses into argv as
  `container-infra-exit` and one on an exit code the runner never uses as `container-exit-unknown`, where both said
  `infra` before (their messages, "infra failure, container exit 1" and "unknown container exit 42", were flattened).
  Both fit the shape. A forge host's untagged `InfraRetry` (its message) and a throw that is not an `InfraRetry` (no
  `reason`) still reach argv as `infra`, though the run record says `worker-error` for them
